newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis enters tense endgame.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis enters tense endgame.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis appeared to enter a tense endgame on Tuesday as President Alberto Fujimori and top aides predicted a bloodless end to the two-week-old stand-off, but declined to rule out military action totally.

As 83 hostages and a score of Marxist rebels spent their 14th straight night holed up in the residence of the Japanese ambassador to Peru in Lima, Fujimori said "several options" were under discussion with the rebels.
"I believe that in the end reason will impose a solution without the spilling of blood, fully respectful of the human rights of the hostages and hostage-takers," he told the Spanish news agency EFE.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was confident of the Peruvian government's ability to handle the crisis -- so much so that he was going ahead with a five-nation Asian trip next week that officials had earlier said might be cancelled.
"My decision to go ahead with the trip is a way to clearly express our trust in the Peruvian government," Hashimoto told reporters.

Hashimoto said he did not think the crisis would necessarily be over by the time he starts his trip on Jan. 7, but added that slow progress was a sign that Peruvian authorities were working for a peaceful solution.

Guerrillas of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) burst into the residence on Dec. 17 during a reception in honour of Japanese Emperor Akihito, taking some 500 hostages and initially threatening to shoot them if 400 jailed colleagues were not freed.

In the interview, made available to Reuters in Madrid, Fujimori said he would not free any MRTA members from Peru's prisons. He said that if his government was to rule out the use of force, the rebels must put down their weapons and free the hostages to a "commission of guarantors".

He gave no other details of the talks under way with the rebels, but appeared to strike a far more conciliatory tone than in a blunt, two-minute speech nine days ago which had been his only previous public response to the crisis.
In an apparently concerted government effort to suggest the stand-off will not end in bloodshed, Fujimori's Prime Minister, Alberto Pandolfi, on Monday also struck a less hardline tone.

"We are sure that the continuing sound handling of the situation will allow a solution that protects the physical well-being and lives of all of the hostages," Pandolfi said in a speech. "The government is working permanently with prudence and dedication for the prompt release" of the hostages."

Despite hopes for a peaceful resolution to the crisis, Peruvian anti-terrorism police sources said crack troops had completed their preparations for a possible assault on the residence if needed as a last resort.

The rebels on Saturday issued a statement via a released hostage, following more than three hours of talks with government negotiator Domingo Palermo, in which they appeared to drop their demand for the release of their jailed colleagues and instead concentrate on improving their living conditions.
Peru's prison regime for those found guilty of "terrorism" has been described by human rights groups as especially harsh.

Palermo, whose visit to talk with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa in the besieged residence on Saturday was the first known face-to-face encounter between an active guerrilla group and a Fujimori administration official, won the release of 20 hostages, leaving 83 in the MRTA's hands.
They had previously released more than 420 hostages.

Palermo and International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Minnig went to the environs of the residence again on Monday, raising speculation that a new release was about to take place.
A bus drew up similar to the ones that have taken away freed hostages on previous days. But Palermo did not meet the rebels and later left without comment to waiting journalists.
The remaining hostages included three ambassadors, dozens of Japanese businessmen and most of the top brass of Peru's police and intelligence forces.

Police Col. Fernando Zapata then told journalists, who so far have been kept at least two blocks away from the residence by police cordons, that photographers and television camera crews would be allowed to approach the entrance to the compound on Tuesday in small groups for an unspecified purpose.
The offer was first made on Monday at the time of Palermo's visit to the compound, raising speculation that the rebels wanted to make a statement directly to the world press, but was then withdrawn.

In what diplomats saw as an attempt by the guerrillas to portray themselves as respectable negotiating partners, the international spokesman of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) on Monday condemned a "solidarity" bomb attack on the Peruvian embassy in Athens.
A group identifying itself as the Guerrilla Fighting Group claimed credit for the attack, in which one woman was injured.
"We reject this sort of display of solidarity because it does not contribute to the solution of a crisis," Isaac Velazco told Reuters in a telephone interview from Hamburg, Germany.
